mainTopic: Damaging oxen and liens: selling, consecrating or slaughtering an ox that did damage, the difference between a תם and a מועד, and the rule that damaging another person's lien is exempt
overview: The גמרא finishes רבא's question to רב נחמן: can an owner sell an ox that did damage, when the ניזק has a claim on it? רב נחמן says the ניזק still collects the ox from the buyer, and 'sold' only lets the buyer plow with it in the meantime. This works because a goring ox counts like an אפותיקי, and everyone knows about it, since people call it 'the goring ox.' Next, a ברייתא of רב תחליפא says selling the ox fails but making it הקדש works. The גמרא shows that this fits both רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא, using the ניזק's lien and רבי אבהו's decree about פדיון. Another ברייתא then contrasts a שור תם, which pays only from its own body, with a שור מועד, which pays from the owner's best property. That contrast decides whether the owner's sale, הקדש, slaughter or gift, and creditors' collection, take effect. Explaining the slaughter ruling, רב שיזבי says the owner is exempt for the value lost by slaughtering. From this, רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע learns that one who damages another person's lien is exempt, even for serious damage. Finally the גמרא asks why creditors lose the תם ox even when their loan came before the damage, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Can the owner sell an ox that is tied up for the injured party?
steps.stepSummary: The end of רבא's question: the damaging ox is liened to the ניזק, so maybe the owner has no power to sell it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the ox is liened to the injured party, maybe it is not in the owner's power to sell it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question רבא asked רב נחמן. If an ox did damage and the owner sold it, does the sale work?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ניזק has a claim on this ox (a שעבוד), because he collects his damages from it. The question is whether that claim blocks the owner from selling the ox to someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: liened / tied up as security for a debt
the injured party
it is not in his power

phrases.english: since it is liened to the injured party –
is it not in his power [to sell it]?
phrases.notes: Literally 'not everything is like him', meaning he has no power to do it.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the ניזק's lien on the ox stop the owner from validly selling it?

steps.title: רב נחמן: the ox is not sold
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that the sale does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is not sold.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers רבא's question. The ox is not sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן holds that the ניזק's claim is strong enough to block the sale. The owner cannot take the ox away from the ניזק by selling it.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not sold (the sale does not take effect)

phrases.english: He said to him: It is not sold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sale is not effective; the ox is not sold.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the ox is sold
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב נחמן with a ברייתא that says if he sold it, it is sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: If he sold it, it is sold!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's answer with a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן said the sale does not work. The ברייתא says plainly 'it is sold', so it looks like a direct contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: but it was taught in a ברייתא (introduces a challenge)
if he sold it, it is sold

phrases.english: But it was taught: If he sold it, it is sold!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's answer in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the ox is not sold.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly says the sale is valid.

steps.title: The injured party still takes it back
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that even so, the ניזק goes and collects the ox from the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: He then collects it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן defends himself. Even if the ברייתא calls it 'sold', the ניזק can still take the ox from the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן reads 'it is sold' in a weak way. The sale exists on paper, but the ניזק's claim still wins and he collects the ox from the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: he goes back and collects it (from the buyer)

phrases.english: He then goes back and collects it.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the injured party, and he collects the ox from the buyer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the meaning of the ברייתא's ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means the sale fully works and the ניזק loses his claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sale works, but the ניזק still collects the ox from the buyer.

steps.title: Then what does 'sold' even mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the ניזק takes the ox back anyway, in what way is it 'sold'?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since he goes back and collects it, in what sense is it sold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes on רב נחמן's answer. If the ניזק takes the ox anyway, the word 'sold' in the ברייתא seems to mean nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sale that can be undone by the ניזק at any time looks useless. So why would the ברייתא bother to say 'it is sold'?

keyTerms.meaning: since / given that
for what (purpose)

phrases.english: But since he goes back and collects it,
for what is it sold?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the sale works but the ניזק collects anyway.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ניזק takes it, the word 'sold' has no practical meaning.

steps.title: It is sold for plowing
steps.stepSummary: The sale counts for plowing. The buyer may use the ox until the ניזק collects it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'sold' means the buyer gets to plow with the ox until the ניזק comes to take it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sale has a real but limited effect. The buyer may use the ox in the meantime, and he does not have to pay the ניזק for that use.

keyTerms.meaning: plowing

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב נחמן, the ניזק's claim stays on the ox even after it is sold. 'Sold' only means the buyer may use it for plowing until the ניזק collects it.

phrases.english: For plowing.
phrases.notes: The buyer may plow with the ox until the injured party comes to take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the word 'sold' a narrow practical meaning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Sold' has no meaning if the ניזק collects anyway.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Sold' means the buyer may use the ox for plowing until it is collected.

steps.title: Does this prove creditors collect from sold מטלטלין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether this ruling proves that a court collects a debt from movable items the borrower sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we learn from this: a borrower who sold movable property — the court collects for the creditor from it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to draw a wide rule from the ox case. Maybe any creditor can collect from מטלטלין the borrower already sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox is like a debt the owner owes the ניזק, and the ניזק collects it even after a sale. If so, maybe every creditor can take back sold מטלטלין from the buyer. That would be a surprising rule, because normally sold מטלטלין are not collected.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from this
borrower
movable property
the court collects

phrases.english: Learn from this:
one who borrows and sells movable property –
the court collects for him from them?
phrases.notes: 'For him' means for the creditor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a general rule on top of the ox ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the ox ruling prove that creditors collect from מטלטלין the borrower sold?

steps.title: The ox is different: it is like an אפותיקי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The damaging ox is treated as if the owner set it aside as an אפותיקי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because it is as if he made it an אפותיקי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks the proof from step 7. The ox case cannot teach a rule about ordinary debts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ניזק collects from this ox specifically, so the ox counts like an אפותיקי. A designated item can be collected even after it is sold. Ordinary מטלטלין that were never designated cannot be collected from a buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: it is different there
an item specifically set aside to pay a debt
it is considered as if...

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying creditors collect from sold מטלטלין in general. Only the ox, which counts as an אפותיקי, is collected.

phrases.english: It is different there,
as it is like one who made it a designated payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects stretching the ox ruling to all sold מטלטלין.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ox is treated as an אפותיקי, unlike ordinary property.

steps.title: רבא says a creditor cannot collect a sold ox that was an אפותיקי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites רבא: a creditor collects a sold slave that was an אפותיקי, but not a sold ox. That contradicts step 8.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבא said: If he made his slave an אפותיקי and sold him, the creditor collects from him. If he made his ox an אפותיקי and sold it, the creditor does not collect from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 8, using a ruling of רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said the ox can be collected because it is like an אפותיקי. But רבא rules that even a real אפותיקי ox cannot be collected once it is sold. So the אפותיקי idea does not seem to explain why the ניזק collects the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't he say (introduces a challenge)
his slave
creditor
collects from it

phrases.english: But didn't Rava say:
if he made his slave a designated payment and sold him –
the creditor collects from him.
[If he made] his ox a designated payment and sold it –
the creditor does not collect from it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation given in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the damaging ox can be collected from a buyer because it is like an אפותיקי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא rules that an ox made into an אפותיקי cannot be collected once it is sold, so being an אפותיקי should not let the ניזק collect it.

steps.title: A goring ox is publicly known, just like a slave
steps.stepSummary: רבא's reason for the slave rule is publicity. A goring ox also has publicity, so it can be collected from a buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why can a slave be collected from a buyer? Because people talk about it. This ox too: once it gores, people talk about it. They call it 'the goring ox.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from רבא in step 9. It explains that a goring ox fits the reason behind the slave rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא allowed collecting a sold slave because people know when a slave is set aside as an אפותיקי, so the buyer was warned. A regular ox has no such publicity. An ox that gored does, because everyone calls it 'the goring ox,' so it is treated like the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'a voice': publicity, something people talk about
A goring ox
A slave

steps.whatToRemember: The buyer loses the ox because its goring is public knowledge, so he knew about the claim on it.

phrases.english: A slave, what is the reason?
phrases.notes: This is the slave from רבא's rule in the last step, which a creditor can collect from a buyer.

phrases.english: Because it has publicity;
This one too, since it gored,
it has publicity,
for they call it 'the goring ox.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from רבא raised in step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying the reason behind the rule: a goring ox shares the slave's publicity
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An ox, like any movable item, has no publicity, so it cannot be collected from a buyer
steps.terutzMaskana: A goring ox is widely known, so it is like the slave and can be collected from a buyer

steps.title: רב תחליפא's ברייתא: sale fails, הקדש works
steps.stepSummary: רב תחליפא teaches before רבי אבהו that if he sold the goring ox, it is not sold, but if he made it הקדש, it is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב תחליפא from ארץ ישראל taught before רבי אבהו: If he sold it, it is not sold. If he made it הקדש, it is הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the ox that gored. This sets up the next question about who is doing the selling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא splits the case in two. A sale does not work, but making the ox הקדש does. It does not say who 'he' is, and the גמרא will now ask about that.

keyTerms.meaning: He sold it
He made it holy (gave it to the בית המקדש)
'The West,' meaning ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rav Tachlifa from the West taught
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

phrases.english: before Rabbi Abbahu:
If he sold it, it is not sold,
if he made it הקדש, it is הקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי רַב תַּחְלִיפָא בַּר מַעְרְבָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about the same goring ox
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling the goring ox does not work; making it הקדש does

steps.title: Who sold it? If the owner, the ברייתא is split between two תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who sold the ox. If it was the מזיק, the first half follows רבי עקיבא and the second half follows רבי ישמעאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who sold it? If you say the מזיק, whose view is 'if he sold it, it is not sold'? It is רבי עקיבא, who says the ox was already handed over. But 'if he made it הקדש, it is הקדש' fits רבי ישמעאל, who says the ox is valued in court!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who the 'he' in the ברייתא is. It tries the first option, the owner of the goring ox, and finds a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא holds the ox already partly belongs to the ניזק, so the owner cannot sell it. רבי ישמעאל holds the ox still fully belongs to the owner, which is why his הקדש works. So the two halves of one ברייתא would follow two different תנאים, which is hard to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who did the damage (the owner of the goring ox)
The ox was handed over (to the ניזק as part owner)
The ox is valued in court (it stays the owner's until then)
Whose view is this?

phrases.english: Who sold it?
If you say the one who did the damage,
'if he sold it, it is not sold': whose view is it?
It is Rabbi Akiva, who says:
the ox was handed over;
phrases.notes: He means the ניזק already owns a share of the ox, so the owner can't sell it.

phrases.english: but 'if he made it הקדש, it is הקדש':
we have come to Rabbi Yishmael, who says:
the ox is valued in court!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks who the subject of the ברייתא is and tests the first option
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the seller in the ברייתא the מזיק or the ניזק?
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the ברייתא as talking about the מזיק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first half fits only רבי עקיבא and the second half fits only רבי ישמעאל

steps.title: If the ניזק sold it, the ברייתא is split the other way
steps.stepSummary: If the ניזק is the seller, the first half follows רבי ישמעאל and the second half follows רבי עקיבא. Both readings leave the ברייתא split.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is the ניזק? Whose view is 'if he sold it, it is not sold'? רבי ישמעאל. But 'if he made it הקדש, it is הקדש' fits רבי עקיבא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second option, the ניזק, and runs into the same problem in reverse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ישמעאל the ניזק owns nothing yet, so he cannot sell. That same reason should also stop his הקדש. For רבי עקיבא the ניזק already owns a share, so his הקדש works, but then his sale should work too. Again the ברייתא seems to follow neither תנא completely.

keyTerms.meaning: The injured party (whose animal was gored)
'We have come to,' meaning this fits the view of

steps.confusionAlert: The same two תנאים switch sides depending on who the seller is. For the מזיק, רבי עקיבא blocks the sale. For the ניזק, רבי ישמעאל blocks the sale.

phrases.english: Rather, the injured party?
'if he sold it, it is not sold': whose view is it?
Rabbi Yishmael,
'if he made it הקדש, it is הקדש': we have come to Rabbi Akiva!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the second option after the first one failed in step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the ברייתא as talking about the ניזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first half fits only רבי ישמעאל and the second half fits only רבי עקיבא, so the ברייתא is still split

steps.title: The seller is the one who caused damage, and selling fails for everyone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the seller is the מזיק, and the ruling fits everyone. Selling fails even for רבי ישמעאל, because the ox is tied by a lien to the ניזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is talking about the owner of the ox that did the damage, and everyone agrees. 'If he sold it, it is not sold' is true even for רבי ישמעאל, because the ox is tied to the injured person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from step 13. It goes back to the first reading, where the מזיק is the seller, and shows that the first half fits רבי ישמעאל too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said that 'selling fails' fits only רבי עקיבא, who holds that the ניזק partly owns the ox. Now the גמרא says that even רבי ישמעאל, who holds the ox still belongs to the מזיק, agrees the sale fails. The reason is that the ox carries a lien, or שעבוד, for the ניזק's payment, and a buyer cannot take that away.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually. It signals that the גמרא is going back to an earlier option and defending it.
Everyone's opinion; all the תנאים agree
It is liened, tied down as security for a debt
The injured party

phrases.english: Actually, it is the one who caused the damage, and it is everyone's opinion;
phrases.notes: This picks up the first option from step 12, where the owner of the damaging ox is the seller.

phrases.english: 'If he sold it, it is not sold' holds even according to Rabbi Yishmael,
since it is liened to the injured party.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from step 13 by going back to the first reading from step 12 and fixing its first half.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that a ruling thought to fit only one תנא also fits the other, but for a different reason (a lien instead of ownership).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Selling fails only if the ניזק owns part of the ox, which is רבי עקיבא's view.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if the ox belongs to the מזיק, as רבי ישמעאל holds, the ניזק's lien blocks the sale.

steps.title: Consecration works even for רבי עקיבא because of רבי אבהו's decree
steps.stepSummary: The second half, 'if he consecrated it, it is holy', also fits רבי עקיבא. This is only because of רבי אבהו's decree, made so that people will not think הקדש can leave without פדיון.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he consecrated it, it is holy' is true even for רבי עקיבא, because of רבי אבהו. רבי אבהו said: it is a decree, so that people will not say that holy property can leave without being redeemed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by showing that the second half of the ruling fits רבי עקיבא too. Now the whole teaching of רב תחליפא fits everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי עקיבא, the ox partly belongs to the ניזק, so the מזיק cannot really make it holy. Still, the חכמים treat it as holy and require it to be redeemed. Otherwise people would see the ניזק take an ox that was declared holy and think that הקדש can go back out without פדיון.

keyTerms.meaning: Property consecrated to the בית המקדש
A rabbinic decree made as a safeguard
Redemption: paying to take something out of holy status

steps.confusionAlert: 'It is holy' here does not mean the consecration fully works for רבי עקיבא. It works only because the חכמים require it to be redeemed, to protect the respect for הקדש.
steps.whatToRemember: רב תחליפא's ruling fits everyone. Selling fails because of the ניזק's lien (for רבי ישמעאל) or his part-ownership (for רבי עקיבא). Consecration 'works' for רבי ישמעאל by law, and for רבי עקיבא only because of רבי אבהו's decree.

phrases.english: 'If he consecrated it, it is consecrated' holds even according to Rabbi Akiva,
because of the ruling of Rabbi Abbahu;
as Rabbi Abbahu said:
It is a decree, lest people say
that consecrated property can go out without redemption.
phrases.notes: He means that the holiness doesn't truly take hold, but the ox still has to be redeemed so people don't get the wrong idea.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִקְדִּישׁוֹ מוּקְדָּשׁ אֲפִילּוּ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer started in step 14 by fixing the second half of the ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a ruling as a rabbinic decree rather than the basic law, so it does not contradict רבי עקיבא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Consecration can work only if the ox fully belongs to the מזיק, which is רבי ישמעאל's view.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי עקיבא, the consecration is honored only by a rabbinic decree requiring פדיון, so the ruling fits both תנאים.

steps.title: A ברייתא: what the owner does with a damaging שור תם before and after court
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that before the owner of a שור תם that did damage goes to court, selling, consecrating, slaughtering, or giving it away all take effect. After the court case, none of these take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: a שור תם that did damage. Before the owner stood in court, if he sold it, it is sold; if he consecrated it, it is holy; if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift, what he did is done. Once he stood in court, if he sold it, it is not sold; if he consecrated it, it is not holy; if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift, he did nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא on the same topic: what happens when the owner of a damaging ox does something with it. The ברייתא divides the case by time, before the court case and after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dividing line is עמידה בדין, standing in court. Before that, the owner's actions with the ox take effect. After the court rules, the ox is set aside for the ניזק, so the owner's sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift has no effect.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים taught; this introduces a ברייתא
An ox not yet known to gore. It pays half the damage, and only from its own body.
Stood in court; the case was judged
What he did is done; his action takes effect

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
An innocuous ox that caused damage;
before he stood trial,
if he sold it, it is sold; if he consecrated it, it is consecrated;
if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift,
what he did is done.
Once he stood trial,

phrases.aramaic: מְכָרוֹ אֵינוֹ מָכוּר, הִקְדִּישׁוֹ אֵינוֹ מוּקְדָּשׁ,
phrases.english: if he sold it, it is not sold; if he consecrated it, it is not consecrated;
if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift,
he has done nothing at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on the same theme of an owner doing things with a damaging ox, now divided by the time of the court case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before the court case, the owner's sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift of a damaging שור תם takes effect. After the court case, none of them take effect.

steps.title: Creditors cannot take the שור תם ahead of the ניזק
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if the owner's creditors collected the ox first, their collection does not count. This is true whether the loan came before or after the damage, because a שור תם pays only from its own body.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the creditors came first and collected the ox, whether he owed the debt before the ox did damage or the ox did damage before he owed the debt, they did nothing, because the payment comes only from the ox's own body.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes on to a new case, where the owner's creditors seize the ox before the ניזק does. It rules that the creditors' collection does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, an older debt might come first. Here the timing of the loan does not matter, because a שור תם pays only מגופו, from its own body. Since the ox is the ניזק's only source of payment, it is set aside for him, and other creditors cannot take it away.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditors; people the owner owes money to
They came first, got there before the ניזק
From its own body. A שור תם's damage is paid only from the ox itself.

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how strongly a שור תם is tied to its damage. Because it is the only source of payment, the ניזק's right to it beats even a creditor whose loan came earlier.
steps.whatToRemember: A שור תם pays only from its own body. After the court case the owner cannot sell, consecrate, slaughter, or give it away, and creditors can never take it ahead of the ניזק, no matter when their loan was made.

phrases.english: If the creditors came first and collected it;
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets, 'and collected it', is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: whether he owed the debt before the ox caused damage,
or the ox caused damage before he owed the debt,
they have done nothing at all,
because payment is made only from its own body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא from step 16 with a new case: creditors who seize the ox first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creditors who seize a damaging שור תם before the ניזק gain nothing, whatever the order of the debt and the damage, because a שור תם pays only from its own body.

steps.title: A forewarned ox: whatever the owner does with it takes effect
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that if a שור מועד did damage, selling, consecrating, slaughtering, or giving it away all take effect. This is true before or after the court case.
steps.simpleTranslation: A forewarned ox that did damage, whether its owner already stood trial or not: if he sold it, it is sold; if he consecrated it, it is holy; if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift, what he did is done.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves from the שור תם to the שור מועד. It says that with a מועד, every action the owner takes on the ox is fully valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a שור תם, the court case was the turning point: after it, nothing the owner did took effect. With a מועד, the court case makes no difference at all. The reason is given in the next line: a מועד does not pay from the ox's own body, so the ניזק has no claim on this particular animal.

keyTerms.meaning: A forewarned ox that has gored several times. Its owner pays full damages from his own property.
Stood trial; the case was brought to court
What he did is done; the action is valid

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the שור תם case in step 16. There, the court case changed everything. Here, for a מועד, the court case changes nothing.

phrases.english: A forewarned ox that caused damage
whether its owner stood trial
or whether he did not stand trial
if he sold it, it is sold
if he consecrated it, it is consecrated
if he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift
what he did is done.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוּעָד שֶׁהִזִּיק – בֵּין שֶׁעָמַד בַּדִּין, בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא עָמַד בַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from the שור תם to the שור מועד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a שור מועד, any sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift is valid, whether before or after the court case.

steps.title: Creditors who collect a forewarned ox keep it
steps.stepSummary: If the owner's creditors collected the מועד ox first, their collection stands, no matter whether the loan came before or after the damage. A מועד pays only from the owner's best property.
steps.simpleTranslation: If creditors came first and collected it, whether he owed them before the damage or the damage happened before he owed them, what they did is done. This is because the payment comes only from the best-quality property.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא says the creditors' collection of a מועד ox is valid. Then it gives the reason for the whole מועד section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of the שור תם in step 17, where the creditors' collection did not count because a תם pays only from its own body. A מועד pays from the owner's עידית, his best land. So the ניזק has no special hold on the ox, and creditors may take it.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditors; people the owner owes money to
The best-quality property (עידית). Damages are collected from it.
Owed; took on a debt

steps.whatToRemember: A תם pays only from its own body, so the ox is tied to the ניזק. A מועד pays from the owner's best property, so the ox is free and anything done with it takes effect.

phrases.english: If creditors came first
and collected it
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in the printed גמרא but is left out of the corrected wording. The word in square brackets is the corrected reading.

phrases.english: whether he owed them before it did damage
or whether it did damage before he owed them
what was done is done
because the payment is not made
except from the best-quality property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the מועד section of the ברייתא and gives its reason, which mirrors the reason for the תם in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creditors who collect a מועד ox keep it, because a מועד pays from the owner's best property and not from the ox.

steps.title: Selling a תם works only for plowing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ruling in the שור תם section that 'if he sold it, it is sold.' The sale is valid only so that the buyer may plow with the ox until the ניזק collects it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'If he sold it, it is sold.' This means for plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the first half of the ברייתא, about a שור תם before the court case. It starts explaining each ruling, beginning with the sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 taught that the תם ox is tied by a lien to the ניזק, so the sale cannot fully take it away from him. 'It is sold' therefore means only that the buyer may use it for plowing in the meantime. When the ניזק comes to collect, he can still take the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said; a formula that brings back a line from the ברייתא in order to explain it
For plowing; for use as a work animal

phrases.english: The Master said:
'If he sold it, it is sold'
phrases.notes: This goes back to the שור תם before the court case (step 16), not the מועד case just taught.

phrases.english: means for plowing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the מועד section to explain the earlier תם rulings in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a שור תם before the court case is valid only for the buyer's use in plowing, until the ניזק collects.

steps.title: Consecrating a תם works only because of רבי אבהו
steps.stepSummary: The ruling that a consecrated תם 'is consecrated' is explained by רבי אבהו's decree. The holiness does not truly take hold, but a פדיון is still required so that people will not think הקדש can leave without פדיון.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he consecrated it, it is consecrated': this is because of רבי אבהו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next ruling of the ברייתא, about consecrating a תם ox, by pointing back to רבי אבהו's decree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the strict law, the ניזק's lien should block הקדש. But step 15 brought רבי אבהו's decree: even though the holiness does not truly take hold, the ox must still be redeemed with a small פדיון before the ניזק collects it. This keeps people from thinking that holy things can go out with no redemption.

keyTerms.meaning: He consecrated it; made it holy property
An אמורא. His decree requires redemption so that people will not think הקדש leaves for free.
Redemption; buying back holy property with money

phrases.english: 'If he consecrated it, it is consecrated'
is because of רבי אבהו.
phrases.notes: This is the decree brought in step 15: a small redemption payment is needed so people won't think הקדש goes out for free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the תם rulings one at a time.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Consecrating a שור תם takes effect only because of רבי אבהו's decree, and it still needs a small פדיון.

steps.title: Why can't the injured party collect from the slaughtered ox's meat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts that giving the ox away works for plowing. But it challenges the ruling on slaughtering: the ניזק should simply collect from the meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift, what he did is done.' It makes sense that giving it as a gift is valid, for plowing. But if he slaughtered it, let the injured party come and collect from its meat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's ruling that slaughtering a תם 'is done.' The ניזק could still take payment from the meat, so the slaughter should not block him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gift can be explained the same way as a sale: the receiver may use the ox for plowing. Slaughtering has no 'plowing' meaning, so what does 'what he did is done' mean? If the ox is now meat, the ניזק's lien should just move to the meat, and the slaughter takes nothing away from him.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense that; a formula that grants one point before challenging another
He slaughtered it
Let him come and collect payment

phrases.english: 'If he slaughtered it or gave it as a gift,
what he did is done';
it makes sense that if he gave it as a gift,
what he did is done, for plowing;
but if he slaughtered it,
let the injured party come and collect from its meat!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא נְתָנוֹ בְּמַתָּנָה, מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה עָשׂוּי – לְרִדְיָא; אֶלָּא שְׁחָטוֹ – לֵיתֵי וְלִשְׁתַּלַּם מִבִּשְׂרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining selling and consecrating, the גמרא reaches the slaughter ruling and finds it hard to explain.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that slaughtering a שור תם before the court case is 'what he did is done.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'for plowing' explanation works for a sale or a gift, but not for slaughtering. Since the ניזק can still collect from the meat, the slaughter seems to change nothing for him.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the ניזק collects even from a slaughtered ox
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from the פסוק that the ניזק is paid from the ox whether it is alive or slaughtered.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: the פסוק says 'live'. That only covers a live ox. How do we know the rule also applies if he slaughtered it? The פסוק says 'and they shall sell the ox', meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge from step 22 with a ברייתא. The ברייתא proves the ניזק collects from the ox even after it was slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ניזק collects from the meat anyway, slaughtering does not hurt him. So why would the ברייתא from step 16 need to tell us that slaughtering the ox 'works'? This source makes the question in step 22 even stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches; introduces the proof from the תורה's wording
He slaughtered it
In any case, whatever the situation
From where do we know?

phrases.english: As it is taught: 'live'
phrases.notes: שמות 21:35: 'they shall sell the live ox.'

phrases.english: I would only know about a live ox
If he slaughtered it, from where do we know?
The verse says: 'and they shall sell the ox'
meaning in any case.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא reads 'the ox' as covering any ox, live or slaughtered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the challenge of step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That the ניזק collects from the ox's meat even after slaughter, so slaughter seemingly needs no special ruling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading the פסוק 'ומכרו את השור' (שמות 21:35).

steps.title: The ruling teaches that the owner is exempt for the value lost by slaughtering
steps.stepSummary: רב שיזבי says the ברייתא's ruling is needed for the drop in value caused by slaughtering.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שיזבי said: the ruling is needed only for the loss in value caused by the slaughter.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שיזבי answers the challenge. The ברייתא is teaching something new about the value lost when the ox was slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slaughtered ox is usually worth less than a live one. 'It is slaughtered' means the slaughter stands, and the owner does not have to make up the lost value to the ניזק. The ניזק just collects from the meat as it is now.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for; shows what a ruling really comes to teach
The loss in value caused by slaughtering

phrases.english: Rav Sheizevi said:
It is needed only for the loss in value from slaughtering.
phrases.notes: He means the owner does not pay the ניזק for the value the ox lost by being slaughtered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 22-23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the ruling a new purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling 'it is slaughtered' seemed to add nothing, since the ניזק collects from the meat anyway.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling teaches that the owner is exempt for the value lost through slaughter.

steps.title: Damaging something liened to another person is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע learns a general rule from רב שיזבי's answer: one who damages another person's lien is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא the son of רב יהושע said: this shows that one who damages property liened to someone else is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע draws a general rule from the case of the slaughtered ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox was liened to the ניזק, since he had a right to collect from it. The owner lowered its value by slaughtering it and is still exempt. So damaging something that only has another person's lien on it is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: This shows; introduces a rule learned from an earlier ruling
A lien; a person's legal right to collect from someone else's property
One who causes damage
Exempt, does not have to pay

steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes a general rule in דיני ממונות: harming another person's lien, as opposed to his actual property, is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua said:
This shows
that one who damages another's lien is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a general rule on רב שיזבי's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who damages property liened to another person is exempt.

steps.title: Isn't this rule obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב הונא needed to say a rule that already follows plainly from the case.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא: his rule seems to add nothing new. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know the owner is exempt for the loss from slaughter, the rule about damaging a lien seems to follow by itself. So why state it?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious; asks why something needed to be said

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether step 25 says anything new.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's rule in step 25.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule seems to be the same thing רב שיזבי already taught, so stating it is unnecessary.

steps.title: The rule covers every kind of damage to a lien, not only slaughter
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought slaughter is exempt only because it takes nothing physical. רב הונא teaches that all damage to a lien is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: only there is he exempt, because he can tell him, 'I took nothing from you. I only took the breath of life from your ox.' But in other cases he should be liable. So רב הונא teaches us that he is always exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' challenge. It shows what mistake we might have made without רב הונא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slaughtering leaves the body of the ox whole. Only its life is gone. So we might have thought the exemption is special to slaughter, and other damage to a lien is liable. רב הונא teaches that damage to someone's lien is exempt in all cases.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said; introduces a mistaken assumption
Breath, the spirit of life
It teaches us; shows what the ruling adds
Merely; or in general, depending on context

steps.whatToRemember: One who damages another's lien is exempt. This is true for every kind of damage, not only slaughter, which merely 'takes the life' of the ox.
steps.confusionAlert: The word בעלמא appears twice with two different meanings. First it means 'merely' (merely breath). Then it means 'in general' (in other cases).

phrases.english: You might have said
that only there is he exempt, because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case of slaughtering the ox.

phrases.english: I have not taken anything at all from you
since he can say to him:
I merely took the breath of life from you
but in general he should be liable
So he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a mistaken assumption the rule rules out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only slaughter is exempt, because it removes nothing physical. Other damage to a lien would be liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any damage to another's lien is exempt.

steps.title: רבה already taught this rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רב הונא's rule, that damaging a lien is exempt, was already said by רבה about burning someone's documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: This rule was also said by רבה. רבה says: someone who burns another person's loan documents is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא again. Why did he need to say this rule when רבה already said the same thing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loan documents let the lender collect from the borrower's property, so they are like a lien. רבה exempts someone who burns them. That looks exactly like רב הונא's rule that damaging a lien is exempt, so his statement seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Documents, here loan documents that record debts owed to the owner
One who burns
Exempt from paying

phrases.english: This too, Rabba already said it,
phrases.notes: 'This' means רב הונא's rule from the last steps: one who damages a lien is exempt.

phrases.english: as Rabba says:
One who burns another person's documents
is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 27 explained why רב הונא's rule was needed beyond the slaughter case, the גמרא now claims רבה already taught it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע's rule that one who damages a lien is exempt
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Repetition: רבה's ruling on burning documents already covers damage to a lien, so a second statement seems unneeded.

steps.title: Even serious damage to a lien is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבה's case could be seen as minor damage, 'just paper'. רב הונא teaches that even serious damage, like digging pits in the land, is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that only in רבה's case is he exempt, because the burner can say: 'I just burned your paper.' But if someone dug pits, ditches and caves in land that has a lien on it, he should be liable. So רב הונא teaches us that slaughtering the ox is like digging pits, ditches and caves, and still the ברייתא says: what he did is done.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב הונא adds something new: even big, real damage to a lien is exempt, not only small damage like burning paper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With burnt documents, the burner can say he only destroyed a piece of paper. Digging pits in the land itself is much more serious, so we might think that is liable. Slaughtering the ox is serious damage like digging pits, and the ברייתא still exempts it ('what he did is done'), so רב הונא teaches that all damage to a lien is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (sets up a mistaken idea we could have had)
Just paper
Pits, ditches and caves, serious digging damage to land
He teaches us
What he did is done; the act stands and he does not pay

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's rule goes further than רבה's. Not just small damage to a lien (burning paper) but even serious damage (like slaughtering the ox, or digging pits in land) is exempt.

phrases.english: You might have said
that it is only there that he is exempt, because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'There' means רבה's case of burning documents.

phrases.english: I just burned your plain paper;
but where he dug in it
pits, ditches and caves,
he should be liable;
so he teaches us
that here it is like one who dug in it
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the case of slaughtering the ox.

phrases.english: pits, ditches and caves,
and still it says: what he did is done.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 28 by showing that רב הונא's rule reaches further than רבה's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the rule adds something new: it covers serious damage, not just minor damage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Damaging a lien is exempt only when the damage is small, like burning 'just paper'; serious damage such as digging pits in the land should be liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Slaughtering the ox counts as serious damage, and it is still exempt, so all damage to a lien is exempt.

steps.title: Creditors who seize the ox first gain nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the ברייתא: if creditors collected the ox first, they gain nothing, whatever the order of debt and damage, because damages are paid only from the ox itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If creditors came first and collected the ox, then whether the owner owed the debt before the ox did damage, or the ox did damage before he owed, they have done nothing, because he pays only from the ox's body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next ruling in the ברייתא it has been studying. This sets up a question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox here is one that is not known to gore, so damages are paid only from the ox itself. The ברייתא says that when the ox's owner also owes money to creditors and they grab the ox first, the ניזק still takes it. This is true even when the loan came before the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditors, people the owner owes money to
Owed, took on a debt
Did damage
Did nothing at all; the act has no effect
From its body, meaning from the ox itself

phrases.english: If creditors came first
and collected it;
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'lifted it' (round brackets); the corrected wording in square brackets says 'collected it' as payment.

phrases.english: whether he owed before it did damage,
or it did damage before he owed,
they have done nothing,
because he pays only from its body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion of the slaughter clause is finished. The גמרא now quotes a new clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creditors who seize the ox before the ניזק gain nothing, whether the debt or the damage came first, because damages are paid only from the ox itself.

steps.title: If the debt came first, the creditor was there first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the ruling when the damage came first, but asks why the creditor loses when the debt came before the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense where the ox did damage before he owed, since the ניזק came first. But where he owed before the ox did damage, the creditor came first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's ruling in one of its two cases, the case where the loan came before the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally whoever has the earlier claim wins. When the damage came first, the ניזק's claim is earlier, so the ruling makes sense. When the loan came first, the creditor's claim is earlier, so why should the ניזק take the ox from him?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (accepts one case before asking about another)
The damaged party
Came first

phrases.english: It makes sense where it did damage before he owed:
the damaged party came first.
But where he owed before it did damage,
the creditor came first!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling just quoted in step 30, but only in its 'debt came first' case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that creditors gain nothing even when the debt came before the damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier claim should come first. When the loan came first, the creditor's lien on the ox is earlier, so he should keep it.
